extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, historians of science, mathematicians interested in historical and cultural aspects of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or evaluating scholarly work in the history of mathematics (conference abstracts, articles) focused on early 20th-century mathematical culture, methods, and institutional history. Emphasis on historiographic argument, use of primary sources, and situating mathematical ideas in cultural and institutional contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hahn’s methodological values (Allgemeinheit, Einfachheit, Strenge, Anschauungskritik)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hahn advocated the values of abstract formulation, simplicity, rigor and criticism of intuition — phrased as “Allgemeinheit”, “Einfachheit”, “Strenge”, “Anschauungskritik”. These were presented not merely as personal style but as ideals for the whole of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embodying these values can involve simplifying proofs, generalizing results, and presenting a single approach that subsumes older ones. The page gives the example that Hahn reworked colleagues' results to simplify and generalize them. Anti-pattern: claiming these values rhetorically without delivering (early Hahn papers contained imprecise terms and results less general than claimed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and accessibility of mathematical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical results and theorems should be presented so that they are understandable from the introduction or with minimal reading; precise definitions (e.g., of 'neighbourhood') should be supplied so the main theorem can be followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts Hahn’s earlier work (where the theorem was not understandable without reading every line) with later work (1906 article) where the final result could be understood after reading the introduction. Avoid scattered systems of equations, vague terms, or the necessity to read the whole article to comprehend the main claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest and accurate claims of generality
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author claims that a result is more general than earlier work, that claim should be supported by the actual scope of hypotheses and proofs; overstatement of generality is a methodological flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes Hahn's tendency to insist on generality and simplicity even when results were not as general as claimed. Evaluate claims by checking whether the stated hypotheses truly cover the asserted breadth; prefer transparent definitions and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful specification of admissible function classes (methodological choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: In disciplines like the calculus of variations, the choice of admissible function classes is a substantive methodological criterion because existence of extrema (and the direction of research) depends on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should justify the class of functions they admit and examine how that choice affects existence and solvability. The page suggests such choices influenced Hahn’s shift toward functional analysis; methodological clarity here can shape later theoretical developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programmatic aims for applied mathematics (practical vs. pure emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied mathematics initiatives and societies can be judged by whether they prioritize practical mechanics/engineering concerns or the modification and application of pure mathematics to practical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The debate between Prandtl (mechanics/practical work, avoid domination by mathematicians) and von Mises (modify pure mathematics for applications) illustrates that institutional aims and journal programs should be explicit about their orientation. Evaluate societies/journals by stated aims, editorial choices, and contributed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and rhetorical role of journals and societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and learned societies shape disciplinary formation; their names, articles, and programs indicate whether they seek to integrate or separate applied and pure strands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how editorial programs, founding debates, and society structures (e.g., GAMM, ZAMM) encouraged or impeded the formation of communities. The text cites the failure to reach agreement on the society’s name/articles as evidence that conflicting aims can impede institutional formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of history as a rhetorical device to situate mathematics culturally
rubrics_metrics.description: History of mathematics can be used not only narratively but rhetorically to argue that mathematics is integral to human culture and to bridge perceived gaps between mathematics and general culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes an increased use of 'history' and 'culture' in titles/abstracts around 1925 and suggests historians and mathematicians used history to claim mathematics' role in broader culture. Evaluate historical writing by how effectively it connects mathematical development to cultural themes without reducing technical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology of scholarly reactions (approval, appreciative rejection, outright rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate scholarly responses to influential cultural works (e.g., Spengler) can be classified into: approval of general themes with criticism of details; careful but appreciative rejection; and outright rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this typology to analyze intellectual reception: identify which category a given response falls into and what that reveals about disciplinary attitudes. Examples: Heinrich Scholz and Helmut Hasse in the first category; Otto Toeplitz and Paul Riebesell in the second; Otto Neurath in the third.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception and value-criteria for mathematical methods (applicability and institutional context)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical method's reception depends on its demonstrated applicability (especially to mathematical physics), pedagogy (textbooks, monographs), and the institutional contexts that promote or absorb it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fredholm example shows that methods that rapidly find effective applications (hydrodynamics, elasticity) and are championed by local 'promulgators' tend to diffuse into textbooks and education. Evaluate methods by practical impact, community uptake, and cross-national transfer via correspondence, prizes, and archives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of model-building in theoretical physics: conceptual promise vs empirical fit
rubrics_metrics.description: When new conceptual frameworks are proposed (e.g., quantum orbits, gravitational lensing), evaluation should weigh both their conceptual integration into broader theory and their empirical adequacy; failure to explain a phenomenon empirically does not necessarily discredit the conceptual framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Einstein examples show that novel concepts may be proposed to explain puzzling data but later judged inadequate for those phenomena; nevertheless, the concepts can remain fruitful (e.g., gravitational lensing leading to microlensing). Evaluate models by their explanatory power, testable predictions, and longer-term theoretical fruitfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicative/tactical presentation choices (formalism coupling and didactic tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should consider how coupling new formalisms to controversial substantive claims affects reception; using accessible illustrative tools (e.g., spacetime diagrams) can greatly aid comprehension and adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues Minkowski erred by coupling his four-dimensional formalism to a controversial electrodynamics of moving media; later, focusing on spacetime geometry and diagrams made the formalism widely useful. Evaluate exposition by its tactical effectiveness: clarity, appropriate separation of controversial claims from new notation, and use of diagrams to convey unintuitive effects.
